evidence.correctness: Ran `/usr/bin/python3.13 experiments/run.py` into the scratchpad and diffed against experiments/results.txt: identical (results.json unchanged in git status). Recomputed independently in a separate script (scratchpad/buildbot/indep.py, numpy, reading buildbot-taskbook/experiments/taskbook.json directly): eligible crew-hours H1 A 32.15 / G1 A 5.89 / H1 B 67.07 / G1 B 16.05 of 46.4 / 93.43 (match 32.1/5.9/67.1/16.1); ownership rate G1 $4.267/h, H1 $24.00/h and s* at supervision 0.3 = 2.423 (G1), 1.071 (H1), at 0 = 8.873/1.577 (match); framing hours 428215 x 0.166 x 0.55 / 37.856 = 1032.8 (match 1033); ceiling H1 A 32.15 x 37.856 = $1,217 = 0.183% (matches the table, NOT the README headline's $1,237 / 0.19%); an independent 200,000-draw numpy Monte Carlo with a different generator gives P(net>0) 0.148 (G1) and 0.0040 (H1) against 0.151 / 0.004. Sourced inputs (BLS $29.12, NAHB $665,298 / $428,215 / 64.4% / framing 16.6%, G1 $16,000) could not be fetched (bls.gov, eyeonhousing.org, heise.de return 403 through the proxy); the NAHB figures agree with the published 2024 study as recalled and with house-cost's shares. The model's outputs are right; the wrong number is a stale README headline (claims).

evidence.verification: `/usr/bin/python3.13 -m pytest -q tests` -> 8 passed. Four seeded mutations with platform/ci/quality_mutate.py: 3 of 4 SURVIVED. The payload-eligibility filter (model.py:33, == 'yes' -> != 'no', which admits 'out of reach' tasks), dropping the success factor in saving_per_house (model.py:77), and widening the slowdown prior to 0.3-10 (model.py:67, allowing a robot faster than a person) all leave every test green. Only the robot_rate hand-calc test caught its mutant. evidence.claims: Limits and disclaimer are good ('Not a quote, not a safety case', swept-not-measured stated in bold, launch prices flagged, ISO 10218 / ISO/TS 15066 / OSHA named). But: README.md:9 headline says the H1 ceiling is '$1,237 (0.19% ...)' and the best H1 draw '$226', while results.txt and the README's own table say $1,217 (0.18%) and $222; project.json:4 says 'H1 32.7 h' (results: 32.1) and project.json:5 lede repeats 0.19%; README.md:9 calls the scope '48-hour' (46.4). README.md:18 calls house-cost's 2,000 ft2 two-storey reference 'an average house', but house-cost/README.md:24 says that reference is its own choice, 'not the survey's average'. Could not load the served page (marisstella.app 403 through the proxy) to see which version ships; project.json feeds the catalogue.
evidence.fitness: The job: a researcher deciding whether to invest in buildbot-fasten/-carry wants to know what speed and supervision a skill must reach for a stock humanoid to pay. The closed-form s* = w/(rate + f w) answers that cleanly and is reusable. But P(saves money) = 15% / 0.4% is entirely a function of the uniform/log-uniform priors the author chose (README says so), so it is not a finding a reader can build on; and no prior work is cited: construction-robot economic feasibility (e.g. Bock and Linner, Construction Robots, 2016; SAM100 / Hadrian bricklaying productivity claims; equipment ownership-cost practice in Peurifoy et al., Construction Planning, Equipment, and Methods). The break-even itself is a textbook engineering-economics application, sound but not new.
evidence.domain: Compared against the standard equipment ownership-and-operating cost method (Peurifoy et al.; Caterpillar Performance Handbook): ownership = depreciation + investment cost (interest, insurance, taxes, typically 10-20%/yr on average investment ~0.6P) + repairs. robot_rate (model.py:48) has depreciation and an 'upkeep' term but no cost of capital, no salvage and no obsolescence cap (life 10,000 h at 500 h/yr = 20 years for a 2024 humanoid). Adding 10%/yr on 0.6P at 1,000 h/yr moves H1 s* at supervision 0.3 from 1.07 to 0.93 (below 1: the H1 never breaks even at the README's base case) and G1 from 2.42 to 2.28. Scenario C converts NAHB framing-stage dollars to hours at an employee loaded wage, while framing is normally subcontracted at a price that includes the sub's overhead and profit, so C's 1,033 h is an overstatement (flagged as crude by the author). Labour-only, no schedule effect: disclosed.

defects.what: README headline states the H1 ceiling as $1,237 (0.19% of price) and best H1 draw $226 on a '48-hour scope'; results.txt and the README's own table give $1,217 (0.18%), $222, 46.4 h. Stale after a taskbook change (32.7 -> 32.1 eligible H1 hours); project.json summary keeps 'H1 32.7 h' and the lede 0.19%.
project.json summary says 'H1 32.7 h' (results: 32.1) and the lede says 0.19% (results: 0.18%); this text feeds the catalogue page.

Ownership rate omits cost of capital (interest, insurance, taxes on average investment), salvage and obsolescence; with a standard 10%/yr on 0.6P the H1 base-case break-even falls from 1.07 to 0.93, i.e. below human speed.

Three of four seeded mutants in core logic survive: the payload-eligibility filter, the success factor and the slowdown prior bounds are not pinned by any test; no test checks eligible hours or results.txt numbers.
Scenario C's 2,000 ft2 two-storey reference is called 'an average house', but house-cost says it is its own choice, not the NAHB survey's average.

No prior work on construction-robot economics or equipment ownership-cost practice is cited; the P(saves) shares are pure functions of uncited priors, so the novelty and weight of the headline are unclear.

verdict: A small, honest, reproducible engineering-economics sketch: run.py reproduces results.txt byte for byte, 8 tests pass, and every model output I recomputed independently (eligible hours from the taskbook, ownership rate and break-even slowdown, NAHB framing hours, and the Monte Carlo shares with a separate 200,000-draw numpy run: 0.148 vs 0.151, 0.0040 vs 0.004) agrees. The swept-not-measured caveat is prominent. It misses the bar on verification and claims: 3 of 4 seeded core mutants survive (eligibility filter, success factor, slowdown prior), and the README headline quotes a stale H1 ceiling ($1,237, 0.19%) that its own table and results contradict ($1,217, 0.18%), with project.json still saying 32.7 h. A cost engineer would also add cost of capital to the ownership rate, which alone pushes the H1 base-case break-even below 1. No prior construction-robot economics is cited. Does not meet the bar (verification 1, claims 2, median 2).
